Lessons.Title: Solve Problems Involving Arrays
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: solve array situations by interpreting equal rows and writing multiplication equations with a symbol for the missing product, then determine and justify the number. This is independent Edulytics lesson prose grounded in the first-edition 2021 IM Grade 3 Unit 1 Lesson 19; original photos are not embedded.

Warm-up, Number Talk: One Less Group (10 minutes). Mentally evaluate 10×2=20, 9×2=18, 8×2=16 and 7×2=14. Explain why removing one group of two reduces the product by exactly two each time. The teacher elicits strategies, including relating successive facts; a numeric pass alone does not establish number-talk reasoning.

Activity 1, Array of Colors (25 minutes): MLR5 Co-craft Questions must happen before the entire story is revealed. Begin with only 'seven rows' and invite students to generate several mathematically sensible questions and identify what information is still missing. Then the 2021 source reveals seven rows with five crayons in each. Students draw a 7-by-5 array, find 35 crayons, explicitly write the unknown-total equation 7 × 5 = □ (also 5 × 7 = □ if the diagram justifies the factors), and rewrite the equality with the total 35. Teacher assesses question quality, array geometry and explanation.

Activity 2, Tyler's Trees (10 minutes): two source array stories are distinct. A Mexican coconut grove has five rows of nine trees, leading to 5×9=□ and 5×9=45; Tyler's backyard permits two rows of four, leading to 2×4=□ and 2×4=8. The student should show or describe a complete array and explain the role of each factor. If coconut-tree media is shown, use the original publisher under appropriate rights; the public image itself is not copied to Edulytics. MLR8 supports clear discussion of rows, columns and grouping.

Lesson synthesis (10 minutes): compare two forms of each equation, with unknown symbol and with the solved product. Ask how the array's rows, repeated groups and symbols correspond to real objects, then how different strategies can reach the same total. Teacher assesses the source co-crafted questions and student drawings, never treating the displayed integer as a substitute.

Publisher original Cool-down is educator-gated. The separate Edulytics task on three rows of eight seedlings tests total 24 as an independent first-party numeric supplement; it is not certified as a copy or a complete substitute for the source Cool-down.

First-edition 2021 official Student Task Statements PDF is three pages: Number Talk with 10×2, 9×2, 8×2, 7×2; crayon story with two distinct requirements (solve and explain, then array and equation with unknown symbol); and two separate Tyler's Trees contexts, EACH requiring unknown-symbol equation, solution and reasoning. Do not collapse the source requirements into only three scalar products.

Edulytics's first-party MLR5 must first show only 'seven rows' and collect student mathematical questions; the rest of the source story is in an initially closed reveal section so the teacher controls disclosure. The crayon 7×5 model and coconut 5×9 and backyard 2×4 models are independently drawn CSS counting-token arrays, not copies of original source media.

Original 2021 source coconut-grove photograph was visually inspected: contextual plantation with coconut trees but no requirement to copy the photograph or infer exact 5×9 counts directly from the picture. The learning numbers come from the two textual source stories. The original photo remains separate from the independently authored mathematically accurate tree arrays.

2021 lesson accessibility includes MLR8 classroom prompts for using words such as array, as well as Action and Expression with connecting cubes or counters. Teacher reflection identifies students whose ideas have not yet been heard so they can participate in the next lesson. Suggested optional centers are Capture Squares Stage 5 and Five in a Row: Multiplication Stage 1. The teacher-only dialogue and diagram assessments must not be reduced to automatic numeric results.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unknown product in an equation
KeyConcepts.Definition: The number representing the total is initially unknown.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Write both factors and a symbol for the product before calculating; later replace the symbol with the product.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rows as equal groups
KeyConcepts.Definition: An array has equally long rows and columns that connect the factors to the picture.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Count rows and objects per row, then use the full product to check the model.
KeyConcepts.Example: Five rows of nine trees hold 45 trees.

KeyConcepts.Title: Co-crafted mathematical questions
KeyConcepts.Definition: A partially described story admits several questions until enough quantities are provided.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Keep source MLR5 question generation distinct from the later numeric solution.
KeyConcepts.Example: Seven rows alone is not enough to know a total without objects per row.

KeyConcepts.Title: Number Talk relation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each new example has one fewer group of two.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use known products to infer that the next is two less.

WorkedExamples.Title: Count backwards by groups of two
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the products of 10×2, 9×2, 8×2 and 7×2 mentally.
WorkedExamples.Method: Subtract exactly two from the prior product.
Steps: Seven groups give 14; explain why the difference is constant.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews mental approach and regularity.

WorkedExamples.Title: Co-craft questions before crayon count
WorkedExamples.Question: What additional information is necessary after learning only that there are seven rows?
WorkedExamples.Method: Generate questions before revealing the row size.
Steps: Ask how many crayons are in each row.
Once the story reveals five crayons per row, draw 7 complete rows of 5.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Seven rows of five produce 35 crayons.
WorkedExamples.Check: The equation, numeric total, drawn array and co-crafted mathematical questions are separately reviewed.

WorkedExamples.Title: Two tree contexts
WorkedExamples.Question: Compute the coconut-tree totals in a five-by-nine grove and a two-by-four backyard.
WorkedExamples.Method: Write a symbolic total and then the solved full equality for each source situation.
Steps: Multiply five by nine to find 45; write 5×9=45.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 45 and 8 trees with two source-specific equations.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks row/column meaning and diagrams.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Solving from 'seven rows' alone without knowing the group size.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The number of objects in each row has not been given yet.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use MLR5 to identify which missing information the question requires.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source requires an array and multiplication equation with a symbol for the total.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Write the unknown-symbol equation, then the separate solved equation and drawing.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Conflating the Mexican grove and Tyler's backyard.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: They have different factors and products.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Copying the coconut-tree image because the numbers are public.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Mathematical numerical facts and the media-rights status are separate.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Draw an independent first-party array and only refer to original publisher media by citation.

SummaryPoints: 2021 warm-up: 10×2=20, 9×2=18, 8×2=16 and 7×2=14; explain one fewer group.
Original source MLR5 introduces only seven rows, then reveals five crayons per row. Preserve this instructional sequence.
Students draw seven-by-five crayon array and write unknown-symbol equation and solved value 35.
Original two coconut-tree situations are five rows of nine (45) and two rows of four (8), each requiring symbolic equation and reasoning.
Teacher synthesis compares unknown-symbol and numeric equalities, not product-only outputs.
First-party numeric Cool-down is not a copy of the gated publisher task.

Source original contextual photograph and three-page 2021 Student Task PDF were reviewed, while the Edulytics visual models are original. Published learner runtime and teacher-graded dialogue remain separate Stage D/classroom verification.
No tests or CI were run; no Stage D, academic approval, merge or deployment.
Each original source A1/A2 context preserves a symbolic unknown equation, then a distinct full solved equality and teacher-reviewed drawing/representation.
2021 teacher supports MLR8 and Action and Expression; reflection checks whose reasoning was shared; Capture Squares Stage 5 and Five in a Row: Multiplication Stage 1 remain optional.
